(actually a combination of several crosses, and some markers do not
overlap).

messages.subject: genetic map
messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I would like to find out if there is a procedure in Rqtl that estimates a
genetic map AND imputes plausible values for missing marker genotypes. If not,
does anybody know how to go about this?
Help is appreciated.
Frank.
messages.body_snippet:
Hi,
I would like to find out if there is a procedure in Rqtl that estimates a
genetic map AND imputes plausible values for missing marker genotypes. If not,
does anybody know how to go about this?
Hel

messages.subject: Re: genetic map
messages.body_plain:
Yes.  est.map() to estimate the inter-marker distances
(assuming that marker order is correct) and ripple() to study
changes in marker order.  sim.geno() or argmax.geno() to impute
missing genotype data.

karl

messages.subject: histograms (again)
messages.body_plain:
Hi again,
Last time I posted I was trying to figure out how to plot a histogram
per phenotype for an ordinal trait, I have that put together if anyone
wants it's below. I know it might be trivial to put together but it
might save someone some time. It's also the first thing I've ever
written so it might be redundant and sloppy.

My next question is now I'm trying to do something similar for a
continuous trait so we can visualize a more subtle allelic effect on
pheno distribution. Of course, plot.pxg is great but we want to
visualize it as a mini-histogram per allele. I figured taking the
columns of a table of geno, pheno and putting them into table and then
making a histogram/ftable before putting it into barplot would work,
but I can't seem to get the functions to take the first column *and*
the names. Any suggestions? Maybe I should add the names as a new 1st
column?

plot.ords <- function(x, marker, phenotype, graphtype) {
	g <- pull.geno(x)[, marker]
	y <- x$pheno[,phenotype]
	tabl <- table(y, g)
	itabl <- table(g, y)
	colnames(tabl)<-c("A", "H", "B")
	rownames(itabl)<-c("A", "H", "B")
	z<-matrix(colSums(tabl), ncol=ncol(tabl), nrow=1)
	tabl.ratios <- cbind(tabl[,1]/z[,1], tabl[,2]/z[,2], tabl[,3]/z[,3])
*100 # generates percentages
	colnames(tabl.ratios)<-c("A", "H", "B")
	colr<-rainbow(nrow(tabl), start=.33, end=.66, gamma=.6) # graph
colours
	icolr<-rainbow(nrow(itabl), start=.33, end=.66, gamma=.6) # colour for
only the g/pheno graph
	bcolr<-"steelblue" #border colour for graphs

	switch(graphtype,
	ordinal = barplot(tabl, beside=TRUE, legend.text=TRUE, border=bcolr,
col=colr, axisnames=TRUE, main=paste(marker, ": ", phenotype,",\n
Frequency per Genotype"), xlab="Genotypes", axes=TRUE),
	ratio = barplot(tabl.ratios, beside=TRUE, legend.text=TRUE,
border=bcolr, col=colr, axisnames=TRUE, main=paste(marker, ": ",
phenotype,",\n Frequency as % of total per Genotype"),
xlab="Genotypes", axes=TRUE),
	gxp = barplot(itabl, beside=TRUE, legend.text=TRUE, border=bcolr,
col=icolr, axisnames=TRUE, main=paste(marker, ": ", phenotype,",\n
Genotype Frequency per Phenotype"), xlab=phenotype, axes=TRUE))
}

messages.subject: Re: histograms (again)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean:

I usually use the lattice package to draw histograms or boxplot conditioned
on a factor, which could be a marker.

I will first have set in a single data.frame both the pheno and geno data
(e.g. "datos"), and then I would use something like:

library(lattice)
histogram(~pheno|marker, data=datos)

or if I want to condition on 2 markers

histogram(~pheno|marker1*marker2, data=datos)

similarly for boxplots:

bwplot(pheno~marker, data=datos)

or for two markers:

bwplot(pheno~marker1|marker2, data=datos)

etc.

But, I usually prefer plot.pxg!!!
Martín

messages.subject: Re: histograms (again)
messages.body_plain:
Hi Sean:

What I usually do is to copy the data directly from an open excel
spreadsheet. (I also could do something like, assuming DataCross contains
the "Cross data",  Datos=cbind.data.frame(DataCross$pheno,
pull.geno(DataCross)) , but marker alleles will be coded as "1", etc, rather
than "A", etc.)

For example; supose you have an excel-spreadsheet with all your data, both
pheno and geno; the first row containing the variable names (phenos and
genos). Your data will look something like this:

SampleID Pheno1 Pheno2 ...Marker1 Marker2 ...
1                10.1     1.5     ....   A             A  .....
2                  9.5      2.3 ......    A             H   ....
etc.

I select the area with the data (including the first row), copy to the
clipboard ("Ctrl+C") and then in the R-console I will write:

Datos=read.delim("clipboard")
str(Datos)    #Will give you information regarding the data structure
summary(Datos)  # Univariate statistics for quantitative variables and
frequencies for categorical variables (factor)
library(lattice)
histogram(~Pheno1|Marker1, data=Datos)

You might want to order the alleles as "A","H","B".  So you might need to
do, before doing the histogram;
Datos$Marker1=factor(Datos$Marker1, levels=c("A","H","B"))
and repeat this for each Marker or use a loop (for example, assume your
markers start on column 4 of your data and ends in column 20)

for (i in 4:30) Datos[,i]=factor(Datos[,i], levels=c("A","H","B"))

You should look at the R documentation for additional help

Cheers

Martín

messages.subject: Re: titles of subplots in R/qtl
messages.body_plain:
You can use par(mfrow=c(2,2)) to create a panel with four
subplots.  You can use title(main="My title") to add a
title to a plot.  If you want to modify a title that comes
as default, you may have to save a copy of the function to
a file (e.g., with dput()) or make a copy of the function
that is in the R/qtl source and edit it directly.  If you
have a modified version of a function in your workspace, it
will be used in place of the one in R/qtl.

Fine control over graphics is part of why I love R, but you'll
quickly get into a lot of R muck.  I highly recommend purchasing
and reading Venables and Ripley, Modern applied statistics
with S (4th edition).

karl

messages.subject: scantwo
messages.body_plain:
I was trying to  interpret the plot.scantwo, but here is what confused
me:
As far as I understand, we have 3 models, NULL, full and additive
models.  Joint LOD score compares the full model with null model;
Epistasis LOD score compares the full model with additive model;
Additive LOD score compare the additive model with NULL model. We can
also compare the additive model with single QTL model to get the
conditional Addive LOD score or compare the full model with single QTL
model to get the conditional interative model. Is that right? If I am
correct, then the help file of plot.scantwo is has some errors because
the epstasis LOD score is explained in a different way. I am using the
latest version 1.01-9

Another question is about missing genotypes. I know the individuals
with missing genotypes are dropped for scanone, but If 20-30% of
genotypes is missing for certain marker, will it affect the estimation
of the LOD score?

Last question. For a backcross case, if for certain marker, the ratio
of A/H is not 1:1, instead it is about 1:2 or 2:1, and the p-val is
0.005, what I can say about it? ( assume there is few or no missing
genotypes) and what precaution should I take when I do scanone or
scantwo? Or it does not matter?

Can anyone help me out on this? Thanks

messages.subject: Re: scantwo
messages.body_plain:
On Mar 7, 2006, at 3:04 PM, sabrina wrote:

>
> I was trying to  interpret the plot.scantwo, but here is what confused
> me:
> As far as I understand, we have 3 models, NULL, full and additive
> models.  Joint LOD score compares the full model with null model;
> Epistasis LOD score compares the full model with additive model;
> Additive LOD score compare the additive model with NULL model. We can
> also compare the additive model with single QTL model to get the
> conditional Addive LOD score or compare the full model with single QTL
> model to get the conditional interative model. Is that right? If I am
> correct, then the help file of plot.scantwo is has some errors because
> the epstasis LOD score is explained in a different way. I am using the
> latest version 1.01-9

Indeed, there's a typo: the epistasis LOD score is the log10 likelihood
for the full model minus the log10 likelihood for the additive model.

> Another question is about missing genotypes. I know the individuals
> with missing genotypes are dropped for scanone, but If 20-30% of
> genotypes is missing for certain marker, will it affect the estimation
> of the LOD score?

In both scanone() and scantwo(), individuals with missing genotype
data are *not* dropped (except if you use method="mr", which we
recommend
against).  Individuals with missing phenotype data are dropped.

> Last question. For a backcross case, if for certain marker, the ratio
> of A/H is not 1:1, instead it is about 1:2 or 2:1, and the p-val is
> 0.005, what I can say about it? ( assume there is few or no missing
> genotypes) and what precaution should I take when I do scanone or
> scantwo? Or it does not matter?

Such segregation distortion might indicate errors in the genotype data.
If it's real segregation distortion, it has some influence on our
efforts to reconstruct the missing genotype data, and so the
calculations
we are doing are less than idea.  But for the most part, the results of
scanone() and scantwo() should be little influenced by segregation
distortion, as the analyses are conditional on the observed genotypes.
If one had quite complete genotype data and relatively dense markers,
segregation distortion will not affect things at all (except in terms
of the power to detect QTLs: equal allele frequencies results in
greater power).

regards,

Karl Broman wrote:
> On Mar 7, 2006, at 3:04 PM, sabrina wrote:
>
> >
> > I was trying to  interpret the plot.scantwo, but here is what confused
> > me:
> > As far as I understand, we have 3 models, NULL, full and additive
> > models.  Joint LOD score compares the full model with null model;
> > Epistasis LOD score compares the full model with additive model;
> > Additive LOD score compare the additive model with NULL model. We can
> > also compare the additive model with single QTL model to get the
> > conditional Addive LOD score or compare the full model with single QTL
> > model to get the conditional interative model. Is that right? If I am
> > correct, then the help file of plot.scantwo is has some errors because
> > the epstasis LOD score is explained in a different way. I am using the
> > latest version 1.01-9
>
> Indeed, there's a typo: the epistasis LOD score is the log10 likelihood
> for the full model minus the log10 likelihood for the additive model.
>
> > Another question is about missing genotypes. I know the individuals
> > with missing genotypes are dropped for scanone, but If 20-30% of
> > genotypes is missing for certain marker, will it affect the estimation
> > of the LOD score?
>
> In both scanone() and scantwo(), individuals with missing genotype
> data are *not* dropped (except if you use method="mr", which we
> recommend
> against).  Individuals with missing phenotype data are dropped.
>
> > Last question. For a backcross case, if for certain marker, the ratio
> > of A/H is not 1:1, instead it is about 1:2 or 2:1, and the p-val is
> > 0.005, what I can say about it? ( assume there is few or no missing
> > genotypes) and what precaution should I take when I do scanone or
> > scantwo? Or it does not matter?
>
> Such segregation distortion might indicate errors in the genotype data.
> If it's real segregation distortion, it has some influence on our
> efforts to reconstruct the missing genotype data, and so the
> calculations
> we are doing are less than idea.  But for the most part, the results of
> scanone() and scantwo() should be little influenced by segregation
> distortion, as the analyses are conditional on the observed genotypes.
> If one had quite complete genotype data and relatively dense markers,
> segregation distortion will not affect things at all (except in terms
> of the power to detect QTLs: equal allele frequencies results in
> greater power).
>
> regards,

messages.subject: Re: CIM?
messages.body_plain:
Dear Alan,

One can do composite interval mapping in R/qtl.  If you have complete
genotype data at a marker, it can be included as an additive covariate
in scanone() or scantwo().

However, I don't particularly like the automated procedures for CIM
(such as using forward selection to a fixed number of markers), and so
I've not implemented such procedures.  I expect to do this eventually,
but I have a long list of other things that I view as more important.

karl

messages.subject: Re: fitqtl, "get.ests", and the intercept term
messages.body_plain:
Hmm.  I guess I neglected to explain things in the help file.
(And summary.fitqtl() is completely lacking a help file!)

For a backcross, the QTL effects come from coding homozygotes
and heterozygotes as -1/2 and +1/2, respectively.  Thus the intercept
should be approximately the average phenotype, and the QTL effects
are the difference between the two genotype group means.

For an intercross, the additive QTL effect comes from coding the AA,
AB and BB genotypes as -1, 0, +1, respectively; the dominance effect
from the coding -1/2, +1/2, -1/2, respectively.  Thus the additive
effect
here is half the difference between the homozygotes.  The intercept is
again the overall average phenotype.

I hope this helps.

Kind regards,
karl

messages.subject: Re: eQTL
messages.body_plain:
It's no doubt possible to compute FDR, but I've not studied it and
can't suggest how to do it.

How many strains are needed...as always, it depends on the truth
and your goals.

R/qtl can handle RILs, but it's not yet documented.  When you read
in your data with read.cross(), you want to use the argument
genotypes=c("AA","BB") or however the two homozygotes are coded.
Then, once the data have been read, they should appear as a
backcross.  To change the cross type to RIL, use

   class(mycross)[1] <- "risib"

or "riself" for RILs by selfing.

The data will be treated like a backcross, but expanding the genetic
map appropriately.

karl

messages.subject: Re: small effect of QTL
messages.body_plain:
Yes; it's appropriate for quantitative traits with normally
distributed residual variation.  If there's just one locus
with large effect, mapping should be easy.

karl
